opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the interesting thing about the auto research setup is that it has this really nice asymmetry built into it: it's very expensive to *find* a good change, but very cheap to *verify* one. Someone out there might burn a ton of compute trying hundreds of ideas, tweaking the architecture, the optimizer, the data mixture, whatever, and most of that goes nowhere. But at the end of the day, if they come back and say, "here's a commit, and it gets the validation loss down to this number in this fixed time budget," I can just run it and check. That's a very different trust model than, say, a normal open-source project where you have to read and understand every line someone sends you.

So the way I think about it is a little bit like a blockchain-ish structure, though without all the baggage. Instead of blocks you have commits, and the "proof of work" is basically the experimentation people did to find an improvement. You don't need to trust the worker at all. You just need a cheap, reproducible verification step. If the result holds up, it gets merged into the shared frontier, and everyone else builds on top of it.

Now, there are a bunch of practical problems you have to solve. One is that you need the evaluation to be really locked down, because the moment you open this up to untrusted participants, people will try to game the metric. They'll overfit to the validation set, or find some weird loophole in how the timing works, or sneak in something that doesn't generalize. So you want a held-out evaluation the workers can't see, a fixed compute budget, a fixed environment. You basically want to make the only way to win be to actually make the thing better.

Another is security. You're running arbitrary code from strangers, so you need it sandboxed properly. That's sort of a solved-ish problem, but you have to take it seriously.

And then there's the coordination question, which I find the most fun. If you have thousands of agents and people all exploring in parallel, you don't want them all trying the same three ideas. So you want some kind of shared log where everyone can see what was tried, what worked, what didn't, so the swarm explores the space instead of piling up on one spot. In a sense you're building a little research community, except a lot of the members are agents.

What excites me is that it lets anyone with spare compute contribute something meaningful. You don't need to be inside a frontier lab. You point your agents at the problem, they grind on it overnight, and if they find something real, it gets folded in. That kind of untrusted, permissionless collaboration could really scale, and I think it's a glimpse of what research looks like when much of the legwork is done by agents and the humans set up the arena and the rules.

r001.rationale: It describes commits entering a shared frontier, with others building on the result, forming a blockchain-like research structure.

r002.rationale: It identifies the experimentation used to find an improvement as the system’s “proof of work.”

r003.rationale: It contrasts the high cost of finding a change with the low cost of rerunning it to verify the result.

r004.rationale: It says workers need not be trusted because the candidate change can be run and checked by the verifier, and frames the contributors as untrusted participants.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot lately, and I think it's actually one of the more interesting design problems out there right now.

So the basic premise is: you have a research loop. An agent proposes a change to a model, trains it, evaluates it, and keeps the change if the number goes up. That's the auto-research pattern, and it works surprisingly well when you run it on a single box with a single trusted agent. The question is what happens when you want to scale that out, and specifically when you want to let anyone on the internet contribute compute or contribute ideas, and you don't trust any of them.

And the thing I keep coming back to is that this is less a machine learning problem and more a mechanism design problem. The ML part is almost the easy part. The hard part is: how do you build a system where it's cheap to be honest and expensive to be adversarial?

A few principles I'd lean on. The first is that you have to separate proposing from verifying. An untrusted worker can propose anything they want, a code diff, a hyperparameter, a data filter, whatever. But the thing that decides whether it gets merged into the trunk is not that worker. It's a verification step that runs in an environment the worker doesn't control. So the worker says "I got a 2 percent improvement," and the system says "great, show me," and reruns it. The worker's claim is just a hint about what's worth re-evaluating. It's never the ground truth.

The second thing is that the verification itself has to be cheap enough that you can afford to redo it. This is where the whole nanochat style of thinking matters to me. If your training run is a hundred thousand dollars, you can't afford to verify anything, and you end up having to trust people, and trust doesn't scale. If your training run is five minutes on a single GPU, you can verify everything, you can even verify it redundantly across multiple independent parties and take a majority vote. So keeping the unit of research small is actually a security property, not just a convenience.

Third, the evaluation has to be hard to game. This is the classic Goodhart problem. If the metric is public and fixed, people will overfit to it, either on purpose or just because that's what optimization does. So you want held-out evaluations, you want them rotated, you want some of them to be secret, and you want the thing you actually care about to be a little bit of a moving target. In a way the adversarial workers are just doing a more aggressive version of what a well-meaning researcher does, which is optimize the number. So you design the number to be worth optimizing.

Fourth, and I think this is underrated, is provenance. Every artifact in the system, every checkpoint, every diff, every eval result, should have a cryptographic trail back to where it came from and what produced it. Not because you need a blockchain or anything like that, but because when something goes wrong, and it will, you want to be able to say "this regression entered the trunk via this contribution from this worker at this time," and roll it back and quarantine that source. Reproducibility is your audit log.

And then the last thing is that I'd want the trunk to be really conservative. Lots of branches, lots of experimentation at the edges, but the actual thing that everyone's building on only moves when the evidence is overwhelming. It's a bit like how the Linux kernel works, or how Wikipedia works. Most of the chaos is at the periphery, and there's a small set of gatekeeping mechanisms that keep the core sane.

What I find exciting about this is that it starts to look like a kind of scientific community in miniature, except the participants can be humans or agents and you don't have to know which. The protocol doesn't care. And if you get the incentives right, you might actually get something that compounds, where the research loop improves the models, and the models improve the research loop, and the whole thing runs without anyone needing to trust anyone.

I don't think we're there yet. I think the eval gaming part in particular is really unsolved. But I think the shape of the answer is pretty clear, and it's mostly about making verification cheaper than deception.

r001.rationale: The response calls for cryptographic provenance for artifacts and explicitly says a blockchain is unnecessary; it does not describe commits building on earlier commits.

r002.rationale: It discusses experimentation and verification, but does not frame finding successful commits as proof of work in a blockchain-like system.

r003.rationale: It says verification should be cheap enough to repeat, but does not state that verifying a successful code change takes much less work than searching for it.

r004.rationale: It has an independent verification step for untrusted workers’ proposals, but assigns verification to a system rather than proposing trusted workers to verify them.

astra-6.text:
I think the central question is: can you make progress easy to verify, even when producing that progress is very hard? Because if you’re going to have arbitrary workers on the internet, you can’t really trust their reports. Someone saying, “I ran this experiment and it’s better,” isn’t sufficient.

So I’d start with a fairly constrained research environment. You have a baseline, you have an evaluation, and workers can propose changes. What comes back is an artifact—a code change, a configuration, something you can actually run. Then you evaluate it independently, in a sandbox, with a fixed resource budget. The worker is proposing a hypothesis; the system decides whether the evidence supports it.

The tricky part is that your evaluation becomes the thing everyone optimizes against. And that’s true even without malicious workers. If you run enough experiments, you’ll find changes that look good by chance. So you need held-out evaluations, replication, and some way of distinguishing an actual improvement from exploiting the measurement.

I’d also want the experiment history to be shared. The useful output of research isn’t just the winning patch. It’s also knowing which ideas were tried, under what conditions, and what happened. Otherwise you have a thousand workers rediscovering the same dead end.

So I wouldn’t initially design it as a thousand agents all talking to each other. I’d design it around a shared experimental record, concrete proposals, and a verifier. Then the interesting question is how much open-ended research you can fit into that structure before verification itself becomes the bottleneck.

r001.rationale: It mentions a shared experimental history, but does not describe candidate commits building on earlier commits or a blockchain-like structure.

r002.rationale: It discusses workers proposing changes and independent evaluation, but does not frame experimentation as proof of work in a blockchain-like system.

r003.rationale: It says progress should be easy to verify even when producing it is very hard, and describes independently evaluating proposed code changes. This communicates the search-versus-verification asymmetry.

r004.rationale: It proposes a verifier that evaluates changes independently, but does not say trusted workers perform verification.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that you don’t trust the workers; you trust the verification. So you need to structure the research problem so that someone can show up, try an idea, and submit an artifact that you can independently evaluate.

For something like improving a model’s training, that artifact might be a change to the code. The worker says, “Here’s my change, here’s the experiment I ran, and here’s the improvement.” But you don’t take their reported number at face value. You run the experiment yourself, in a sandbox, with a fixed evaluation and a fixed compute budget. And if it actually improves things, you can incorporate it.

The tricky part is defining what “improves things” means. Because the moment you put a metric out there, you’ve created an optimization target. People—or agents—can find ways to make that number go up without making the system better. So the evaluation itself becomes a very important part of the research system. You probably want held-out tests, reproducibility checks, and some way to account for the cost of the improvement.

Then there’s a coordination question. You don’t necessarily want a thousand workers all trying the same obvious thing. You want a shared record of what’s been tried, what worked, what failed, and under what conditions. But I’d start with a very small, concrete loop: take the current best version, propose a modification, run it, verify it, and keep it if it’s better. Get that loop working reliably, and then figure out how to scale the number of people and agents contributing to it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions a shared record of prior experiments, but does not describe a blockchain-like history or candidate commits building on earlier commits.

r002.rationale: It describes proposing and evaluating modifications, but does not frame the search for successful commits as proof of work in a blockchain-like system.

r003.rationale: It says candidate changes should be independently evaluated, but does not compare the effort required to verify a change with the effort required to find it.

r004.rationale: The response proposes independent evaluation in a sandbox, but does not assign verification to trusted workers overseeing candidates from an untrusted pool of internet workers.
